        ⟦MC_ad76f84d9f135f96_0⟧Deadlock⟦MC_b8073d8a2f01abcc_0⟧    
        ⟦MC_2515913aa56874a1_0⟧All are phenomena in which processes cannot move forward smoothly (except for intentionally designed infinite loops)⟦MC_b8073d8a2f01abcc_1⟧
        ⟦MC_ad76f84d9f135f96_1⟧Deadlock is necessarily caused by "circular waiting for the resources held by each other," so if a deadlock occurs, then ⟦MC_507ca5a2742e5330_0⟧at least two or more processes are deadlocked at the same time⟦MC_5a173609876c90d5_0⟧. In addition, processes involved in a deadlock must be in the blocked state.⟦MC_b8073d8a2f01abcc_2⟧
    ⟦MC_3ed7440ce0756928_1⟧
    ⟦MC_9b84c614b473bf1d_2⟧
        ⟦MC_ad76f84d9f135f96_2⟧Starvation⟦MC_b8073d8a2f01abcc_3⟧   
        ⟦MC_ad76f84d9f135f96_3⟧⟦MC_507ca5a2742e5330_1⟧Only one process may experience starvation⟦MC_5a173609876c90d5_1⟧. A starving process may be in either the blocked state (e.g., unable to obtain the required I/O device for a long time) or the ready state (unable to obtain the processor for a long time).⟦MC_b8073d8a2f01abcc_4⟧
    ⟦MC_3ed7440ce0756928_2⟧
    ⟦MC_9b84c614b473bf1d_3⟧
        ⟦MC_ad76f84d9f135f96_4⟧Infinite loop⟦MC_b8073d8a2f01abcc_5⟧    
        ⟦MC_ad76f84d9f135f96_5⟧Only one process may enter an infinite loop. A process in an infinite loop can run on the processor (it can be in the running state); it just cannot move forward smoothly as expected. Deadlock and starvation are caused by unreasonable resource allocation policies of the operating system, whereas infinite loops are caused by errors in code logic.⟦MC_507ca5a2742e5330_2⟧Deadlock and starvation are problems of the manager (the operating system), while infinite loops are problems of the managed.⟦MC_5a173609876c90d5_2⟧⟦MC_b8073d8a2f01abcc_6⟧
